When a database updates the data, it first writes the changes to the write-ahead log. The write-ahead log is a record of all the changes that have been made to the data, in the order they were made. This means that even if the database crashes before it has a chance to update the data in memory, the write-ahead log still contains a record of the changes that need to be made. After the crash, the database can recover by re-applying the changes recorded in the write-ahead log to the data. This ensures that the data is consistent and up-to-date, even if the database crashed.
The write-ahead log serves as a safety net, allowing the database to recover from a crash by re-applying the changes that were recorded in the log. This means that even if the database crashes and some of the changes are not yet written to disk, the write-ahead log ensures that those changes are still applied to the data, preventing the loss of data. ## Step 1: Understand the purpose of a write-ahead log
A write-ahead log (WAL) is a mechanism used by databases to ensure data consistency and durability in the event of a system crash or failure. The primary purpose of a WAL is to record all changes made to the database before they are written to the main database files.

## Step 2: Explain the structure of the log file
The log file is structured as a sequence of log records, each of which represents a single database operation, such as a write or update. Each log record contains a sequence number, the type of operation (e.g., insert, update, delete), and any relevant data required to perform the operation. The log records are written in a specific order to ensure that they can be applied in a consistent manner.
